extracted.intended_audience: attorneys/parties and counsel litigating or defending USPTO OED disciplinary proceedings (practitioners before the USPTO)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria governing summary judgment, burdens of proof, collateral estoppel, discovery-related relief, and practitioner supervision issues in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline proceedings. Focused on how courts evaluate motions for summary judgment and when prior state-court findings may be given preclusive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of Proof in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the OED Director shall have the burden of proving the violation by clear and convincing evidence," while the "respondent shall have the burden of proving any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence." 37 C.F.R. § 11.49.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocation of burdens is explicit: OED Director must prove violations; respondent must prove affirmative defenses—both by the intermediate 'clear and convincing' standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear and convincing evidence is an intermediate standard requiring evidence of such weight that it "produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy, as to the truth of the allegations sought to be established" or "proves the facts at issue to be 'highly probable.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: Jimenez v. DaimlerChrysler, 269 F.3d 439, 450 (4th Cir. 2001); Colorado v. New Mexico, 467 U.S. 310, 316 (1984). Use this standard when assessing whether the OED Director met his burden or respondent met burden on affirmative defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment standard (Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a) as applied by 37 C.F.R. § 11.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may grant summary judgment "if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key authorities: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986); Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986). Define 'genuine' and 'material': an issue is genuine if reasonable factfinder could rule for either party; a fact is material if it can affect outcome under governing law. The court must view evidence in the light most favorable to the nonmovant (Tolan v. Cotton). Summary judgment inappropriate where material facts are susceptible to divergent inferences; appropriate where a party has failed to make sufficient showing on an essential element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moving party's burden on summary judgment (Celotex principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The party moving for summary judgment bears the burden of showing that the material facts are undisputed and that these undisputed facts entitle the movant to judgment as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A movant must identify undisputed facts and explain how those facts warrant judgment; merely asserting lack of evidence from the other side is insufficient if the movant does not show entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: How courts view evidence and inferences on summary judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: On summary judgment, the court must view the evidence in the light most favorable to the party opposing judgment; summary judgment is not available where material facts, though undisputed, are susceptible to divergent inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Tolan v. Cotton, 572 U.S. 650; United States v. Diebold, Inc., 369 U.S. 654; Tao v. Freeh, 27 F.3d 635. When evidence allows reasonable differing inferences, the issue is for the factfinder, not summary disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 56(d) (formerly 56(f)) relief for incomplete discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may deny or defer consideration of a motion for summary judgment if the nonmovant "shows by affidavit or declaration that, for specified reasons, it cannot present facts essential to justify its opposition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain 56(d) relief the nonmovant must identify specific information it seeks that would create a genuine dispute of material fact; blanket or vague assertions that discovery would be beneficial are insufficient. Authorities: McCray v. Md. DOT; Gordon v. CIGNA Corp.; McClure v. Ports; Dufau v. Price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to identify specific facts or information for Rule 56(d) relief
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonmovant must "identify any specific information that would create a genuine dispute of material fact" to justify deferral or denial of summary judgment under Rule 56(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General or vague claims of pending discovery or unspecified defenses will not support 56(d) relief. Courts require specificity as to which facts are expected to be uncovered and how they are material to opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Rule 56(f)/court-initiated summary judgment for nonmovant
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Rule 56(f) (now Rule 56), after giving notice and a reasonable time to respond, a court may grant summary judgment for a nonmovant or consider summary judgment on its own after identifying material facts that may not be genuinely in dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though not governing in USPTO proceedings, Rule 56(f) provides useful guidance on courts granting summary judgment sua sponte for a nonmovant after notice and opportunity to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral estoppel / issue preclusion (Oregon law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Oregon law, a party may be collaterally estopped from relitigating an issue of ultimate fact decided in a prior proceeding if five requirements are met: (1) identical issue; (2) actually litigated and essential to prior final decision on merits; (3) party had full and fair opportunity to be heard; (4) party sought to be precluded was a party or in privity with a party to prior proceeding; (5) the prior proceeding was the type to which preclusive effect is given. (Nelson v. Emerald People's Util. Dist., 862 P.2d 1293.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking offensive collateral estoppel, courts assess each element; a satisfied five-part test supports giving prior judicial findings preclusive effect in USPTO proceedings (Full Faith and Credit via 28 U.S.C. § 1738 requires applying state preclusion law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preclusive effect of default judgments under Oregon law
rubrics_metrics.description: Oregon courts may apply issue preclusion to matters resolved by default judgment; where an issue was resolved via default judgment, analysis should focus on whether the issue was 'essential to the [first] judgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Gwynn v. Wilhelm; Sturgis v. Asset Acceptance. Default judgments can yield collateral estoppel if the issue was essential and the defendant had opportunity to contest; USPTO precedent supports preclusive effect where respondent had opportunity to contest prior state court matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements/facts that may be established via collateral estoppel and used in USPTO proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior judicial findings—e.g., that a practitioner employed unlicensed staff who provided legal advice, failed to supervise them, permitted use of firm name, collected fees without providing services, issued NSF checks—can be adopted as established facts against a respondent through collateral estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED Director may rely on such prior findings rather than re-proving identical factual predicates in the USPTO disciplinary proceeding, provided the preclusion elements are satisfied and the findings are properly presented as exhibits or otherwise in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of state-court documents and Federal Rules of Evidence in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Rules of Evidence are not controlling in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.50(a)); the OED Director may submit copies of documents from other court proceedings as exhibits and need not rely on judicial notice under Rule 201.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If documents are submitted as exhibits and their authenticity is not challenged, the tribunal may consider them even though FRE and Rule 201 procedures differ from federal civil courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing timeliness and good cause for extensions or renewals of dispositive motion deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests to extend deadlines or renew motions are evaluated for timeliness, whether movant had notice of the need earlier, whether the movant caused the delay, and whether outstanding discovery is actually linked to the arguments for which more time is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late requests filed on the deadline without earlier action are disfavored; history of filing meritless motions and self-inflicted defects in discovery/summons weigh against granting extensions. The movant must proffer nexus between outstanding discovery and the summary judgment arguments to show good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity and prerequisites for subpoenas in this forum (Rule 45 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.52 limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subpoenas must be properly signed/issued (Rule 45(a)(3))—for example by the clerk or an attorney authorized to practice in the relevant court—and must comply with the scope of discovery authorized under 37 C.F.R. § 11.52.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improperly issued subpoenas (unsigned or issued by one lacking authority) or subpoenas exceeding the authorized scope may be objected to and rendered invalid; proof of service must be shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: When summary judgment may be granted against a nonmovant who fails to make a sufficient showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary judgment may be appropriate against a party who has failed to make a sufficient showing on an essential element as to which he has the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nonmovant cannot point to specific disputed material facts or produces no contrary evidence where required, the court may enter summary judgment against that party (Celotex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearsay admissibility and Confrontation Clause in USPTO administrative proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearsay is admissible and the Confrontation Clause does not apply in this administrative proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, declarations signed under penalty of perjury (even from witnesses not present) may be admissible evidence; inability to locate a declarant does not automatically require striking related claims if the declaration exists and has been produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 11.503(a)-(b) duty: practitioner responsibilities to supervise non-practitioner assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.503(a) requires that a practitioner who possesses managerial authority make reasonable efforts to ensure the firm has measures giving reasonable assurance that the conduct of non-practitioner assistants is compatible with the practitioner's professional obligations; Section 11.503(b) imposes similar duties on practitioners with direct supervisory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation focuses on whether the practitioner made 'reasonable efforts' to ensure non-practitioner conduct complied with professional obligations (adequate supervision, monitoring, and controls). Failure to do so can support violation findings under 37 C.F.R. §11.503.
